title: First-time visitor tips for Myrtle Beach
summary: Ten things worth knowing before your first trip to the Grand Strand
description: Practical tips for a first trip to Myrtle Beach: where to stay, how the Grand Strand is laid out, how to avoid traffic, what to book ahead and common planning mistakes.
intro: The Grand Strand is about sixty miles of beach running from Little River at the North Carolina line down through Pawleys Island, and the part most people mean by Myrtle Beach is only a slice of it. First-time visitors often assume everything is close together. It is not. These notes are meant to save you from the most common planning mistakes.

sections.h: 1. Know the geography before you book
p: From north to south, the main areas are Little River, North Myrtle Beach, Myrtle Beach itself, Surfside Beach and Garden City, Murrells Inlet and Pawleys Island, with Georgetown a bit further down the coast and Conway inland. Driving from one end to the other can take well over an hour in summer traffic. Pick a base that matches what you want to do, and treat the other areas as day trips. Our areas pages describe each one.

sections.h: 2. Choose your base for the trip you want
p: Central Myrtle Beach puts you near the Boardwalk, the SkyWheel, Broadway at the Beach and most of the family attractions, and it is the busiest. North Myrtle Beach is calmer and has a long stretch of residential beach. Surfside and Garden City are low-key and family-oriented. Murrells Inlet and Pawleys Island suit travelers who want marsh views and good seafood more than nightlife. If you have a car and an itinerary, none of these is a mistake. If you want to walk to everything, central Myrtle Beach is the practical choice.

sections.h: 3. Expect traffic and plan around it
p: Highway 17 and Ocean Boulevard are the main arteries, and both slow down in summer, especially on Saturdays when many rentals change over. Try to do your longer drives early in the morning or after dinner. If you are driving in on a Saturday in summer, build in extra time. Our getting-around page explains the main roads, buses and beach parking.

sections.h: 4. Book the things that sell out
p: You can arrive without a plan for the beach or the Boardwalk. Evening shows, dinner shows, dolphin cruises, escape rooms and some tee times are different: they run on set schedules and can sell out in peak weeks. Book those before you leave, and leave the rest of the trip flexible.

sections.h: 5. Do not skip the free things
p: The beach is free, and so is the Myrtle Beach Boardwalk, which stretches along the oceanfront for more than a mile and is lined with shops, snack stands and rides. State parks charge a small entry fee but offer some of the best scenery on the coast. Our free things guide collects more.

Summer is hot, busy and fully open. Spring and fall are milder and easier, though some seasonal attractions open late or close early. Winter is quiet and cheap, with a smaller list of what is open. Ask before you drive anywhere in the off-season.

sections.h: 7. Bring what you will actually use
list: Sunscreen and a hat. The sun reflects off water and sand, and it is easy to burn on a cloudy day.
Water shoes if you plan to explore marsh or creek edges.
A light layer, even in summer, for air-conditioned theaters and restaurants.
A refillable water bottle. Many attractions are largely outdoors.
Bug spray for evenings near water.

sections.h: 8. Watch for the details on the beach
p: Beach rules differ by town and change over time. In general, you should expect limits on alcohol, glass, fires and dogs, and seasonal rules about tents and equipment. We have a separate page on beach rules and safety. Check the town you are in before you set up.

sections.h: 9. Plan one day away from the beach
p: Even beach lovers enjoy a day off the sand. Brookgreen Gardens and Huntington Beach State Park in Murrells Inlet pair well, and Georgetown has a historic downtown, museums and a waterfront. Hobcaw Barony is a good choice if you like history and nature. Those take you away from the crowds and show a different side of the coast.

The most common regret from first trips is trying to do too much. A beach morning, one main activity and an evening plan is a full day, especially with children. Treat everything else as a bonus. Our itineraries for families, couples, golfers and rainy weekends are built around that idea.
